meta.subject: math
meta.title: Mastering Fractions Visually
meta.summary: See why equivalent fractions, mixed numbers, adding and multiplying work, with pictures you can drag and slice.

chunks.title: What a fraction really means
body: A fraction $\dfrac{a}{b}$ means: cut one whole into **b equal pieces** and take **a** of them.
The bottom number (the **denominator**) tells you the *size* of the pieces. The top number (the **numerator**) *counts* them.
Everything in this chapter comes from that one idea.

chunks.title: Module 1 · The Knife & Glue
intro: Tap ✂️ to cut every piece into smaller pieces.
The **number** of pieces changes, but the **amount** shaded never does.
tasks: Set up $\dfrac{4}{6}$ (top 4, bottom 6), then press **Glue**. What do you get?
Why does the shaded part never change size?

challenges.explain: Each third was cut into 4: $2 \times 4 = 8$ and $3 \times 4 = 12$, so $\tfrac{8}{12}$ is the same amount as $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

chunks.title: Equivalent fractions
body: Multiply (or divide) the top **and** the bottom by the **same** number, and the value doesn't change:
$$\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a \times k}{b \times k}$$
**Simplest form**: divide the top and bottom by their HCF, so that no number except 1 goes into both.

mistakes.why: $\dfrac{6}{9}$ is equal, but 6 and 9 can still both be divided by 3. Keep gluing!
Equal, but not simplest: 4 and 6 can both still be divided by 2.

chunks.title: Module 2 · The Container Overflow Tank
intro: An **improper fraction** has a top that is bigger than (or equal to) the bottom, like $\dfrac{11}{4}$.
Each container holds 4 quarters. Pour in 11 quarters and watch the containers fill up one by one.
tasks: What is $\dfrac{4}{4}$ equal to? Press − until you see it.

challenges.explain: 7 pieces fill 2 containers of 3 with 1 left over, so $\tfrac{7}{3} = 2\tfrac{1}{3}$.

challenges.text: Fill **exactly 3** containers of quarters, with nothing left over.

chunks.title: The shortcut: divide
body: To turn $\dfrac{n}{d}$ into a mixed number, **divide** $n$ by $d$.
The answer is the number of wholes; the **remainder** is the new top.
$$\frac{11}{4}: \quad 11 \div 4 = 2 \text{ remainder } 3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2\tfrac{3}{4}$$
Going back: $2\tfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{2 \times 4 + 3}{4} = \dfrac{11}{4}$.

mistakes.why: 5 goes into 17 **three** times ($3 \times 5 = 15$), not twice. Then $17 - 15 = 2$ pieces are left.
$4 \times 5 = 20$, which is more than 17. Only 3 containers fill up completely.

chunks.title: Why can't we just add the tops and the bottoms?
body: Try $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}$. Lots of people write $\dfrac{2}{5}$.
But **halves** and **thirds** are different-sized pieces.
You can't count them together, just as 1 metre + 1 centimetre isn't 2 of anything.
First, both fractions have to be cut into pieces of the **same size**.

chunks.title: Module 3 · The LCD Grid Merger
intro: Box A is cut into columns, Box B into rows.
Tap **＋** to give both boxes the same grid, then **＝** to pour the pieces together.
tasks: Is $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}$ equal to $\dfrac{2}{5}$? Use the trap box to explain why not.
For $\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{6}$, what is the answer in simplest form?

challenges.text: Add $\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{6}$ all the way to the combined answer.
challenges.explain: Both turned into 24ths: $\tfrac{6}{24} + \tfrac{4}{24} = \tfrac{10}{24}$, which simplifies to $\tfrac{5}{12}$.

challenges.text: Build a sum that spills into a **second box**, then combine it.

chunks.title: Adding fractions
chunks.caption: Only add the **tops** once the **bottoms** match. The bottom names the piece size, so it stays the same.

options.why: Careful! Did you add the denominators straight across? Fifths and thirds are different sizes. Check the Grid Merger above!
You found the common denominator (15) but didn't change the tops: $\dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{15}$ and $\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{5}{15}$.

chunks.title: Module 4 · The Area Overlap Grid
intro: Blue covers $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of the width. Yellow covers $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the height. The green overlap is $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
tasks: Set yellow to $\dfrac{4}{4}$ (all the rows). What happens to the green, and why?

challenges.explain: Half of a half is a quarter: 1 green square out of 4.

challenges.text: Make the green exactly **3 squares out of 20**.

chunks.title: Multiplying fractions
body: Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms: $\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{a \times c}{b \times d}$
No common denominator needed!
When both fractions are less than 1, the answer is smaller than both: you're taking a part **of** a part.

mistakes.why: The multiplying is right! Now simplify: 6 and 15 can both be divided by 3.
You added the tops and the bottoms. To multiply, **multiply** them: $3 \times 2$ over $5 \times 3$.

flashcards.front: What do the top and bottom of $\dfrac{a}{b}$ mean?
flashcards.back:
Bottom: how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.
Top: how many of those pieces you take.

flashcards.front: How do you make an equivalent fraction?
flashcards.back:
Multiply (or divide) the top **and** the bottom by the same number.
$\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{12}$

Divide the top and bottom by the HCF, 6:
$\dfrac{2}{3}$

mistakes.why: You **added** 16 to the top because $4 + 16 = 20$. Equivalent fractions **multiply**: $4 \times 5 = 20$, so the top becomes $3 \times 5$.
5 is the multiplier ($4 \times 5 = 20$). Now multiply the top by it too: $3 \times 5$.

hints: How many times bigger is 20 than 4?
$4 \times 5 = 20$. Whatever you do to the bottom, do to the top.

hints.text: $\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{3 \times 5}{4 \times 5} = \dfrac{15}{20}$. The knife cuts each quarter into 5, so 15 of the 20 pieces are shaded.

mistakes.why: $6 \times 4 = 24$, which is **more** than 23. Only 3 containers fill up completely.

hints: $6 \times 3 = 18$ and $23 - 18 = 5$. So 3 full containers, with 5 pieces left over.

mistakes.why: Careful! Did you add the denominators straight across? Quarters and thirds are different sizes. Check the Grid Merger above!
You made the bottoms match (12) but forgot to change the tops: $\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{12}$ and $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{12}$.

hints: Quarters and thirds are different-sized pieces. What smaller piece could both be cut into?

options.why: Careful! Did you add the denominators straight across? Check the Grid Merger above!
You matched the bottoms (sixths) but didn't change $\dfrac{1}{2}$ into $\dfrac{3}{6}$.

hints: How many sixths make one half?

hints.text: $\dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3} = 1\tfrac{1}{3}$. It's more than one whole, so it spills into a second box.

questions.prompt: A garden covers $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of a field. Vegetables grow on $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of the garden. What fraction of the **whole field** grows vegetables? ___

mistakes.why: The multiplying is right! Now simplify: divide the top and bottom by 2.
You added the tops and the bottoms. *Of* means **multiply**.
That's $\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{2}{5}$. A part **of** a part means multiplying.

hints: The word *of* means multiply. You want $\dfrac{2}{5}$ **of** $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
Multiply the tops and the bottoms: $\dfrac{2 \times 3}{5 \times 4}$.

hints.text: $\dfrac{6}{20} = \dfrac{3}{10}$. The green overlap is 6 of the 20 squares.

items.title: 2 · Simplest form
items.body: Divide the top and bottom by their HCF.

items.title: 4 · Adding (different bottoms)
items.body: Match the bottoms first. **Never** add the bottoms: $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{3} \neq \tfrac{2}{5}$.

items.title: 6 · Trap checklist
body: - Adding or subtracting? Make the bottoms match first.
- Multiplying? No common bottom needed.
- Is the answer in simplest form?
- Top bigger than bottom? Write a mixed number if the question asks.
